register.name: Heat wave
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will go through a heat wave in the next ten years (about 4.5 times a year).

sub_causes.name: A blackout during a heat wave
sub_causes.note: When the power fails in extreme heat, air conditioning fails for everyone at once. It is the most dangerous combination; where it matters most it is a named scenario.

register.name: Medical emergency
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years (about 1.9 times a year).

sub_causes.name: Far from emergency care
sub_causes.note: Ambulances take about twice as long to reach rural homes (a median of about 14 minutes against 7).

sub_causes.name: Falls
sub_causes.note: Falls are a leading reason older adults need emergency care; clear floors and light the way at night.

sub_causes.name: Going into labour during a disaster
sub_causes.note: Labour can start while roads are closed or the power is out. Know two ways to the hospital and pack the go-bag early.

register.name: Cold wave
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will go through a spell of dangerous cold in the next ten years (about once a year).

sub_causes.name: Rolling blackouts in extreme cold
sub_causes.note: Gas supply and power plants fail in deep cold and the grid cuts power in rotation or for days (Texas, February 2021). Already in the county's outage record.

register.name: Wildfire smoke
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 98 (88 to nearly all) will go through days of unhealthy wildfire smoke in the next ten years.

register.name: Phone or internet outage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (63 to nearly all) will lose phone and internet service for hours in a network outage in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: GPS or radio disruption
sub_causes.note: Space weather or jamming can degrade navigation and timing. Keep a paper map for the way home.

register.name: Supply chain disruption
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 86 (63–98) will find store shelves empty of things they need in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Fuel shortage
sub_causes.note: Gas stations run dry for days (the Colonial Pipeline shutdown, May 2021, and before hurricanes). It matters most with a generator or a long drive.

sub_causes.name: Cut off: an island or a single road
sub_causes.note: A bridge, ferry or the only road closes and the community is cut off for days. Plan for longer if that is you.

register.name: Strong wind
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 86 (44 to nearly all) will lose power or have damage in a windstorm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Derecho
sub_causes.note: A fast line of storms with hurricane-force gusts over hundreds of miles; outages can last days. Counted in the windstorm rate.

register.name: Job loss
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 81 will have someone lose a job in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Livestock or poultry disease
sub_causes.note: An animal-disease outbreak (bird flu in dairy or poultry) can hit a farm's income.

sub_causes.name: Recession layoffs
sub_causes.note: Layoffs cluster in downturns; the high end of the job-loss range is a recession year.

register.name: Local water or gas outage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 78 (50–95) will have a water main break or boil-water notice in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Toxic algae in the water supply
sub_causes.note: Algae toxins reach the treatment plant and a do-not-drink order follows (Toledo, 2014). Counted in the water-notice rate.

sub_causes.name: Gas main over-pressure or leak
sub_causes.note: Gas mains over-pressure or leak and homes must be evacuated (Merrimack Valley, 2018). If you smell gas, leave first, then call.

sub_causes.name: Water system failure for weeks
sub_causes.note: A treatment plant or system fails for weeks (Jackson, Mississippi, 2022; Asheville, 2024). The water targets use the county's drinking-water violations to size it.

sub_causes.name: Sewer failure
sub_causes.note: Pumps stop or mains break and toilets cannot be flushed. The sanitation supplies follow the water target.

register.name: Stranded in a vehicle
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 78 (39–98) will be stranded away from home by a crash, breakdown or shutdown in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Black ice or dense fog
sub_causes.note: Chain-reaction crashes and closed highways. Counted in the stranding rate.

sub_causes.name: Transit shutdown or strike
sub_causes.note: Buses and trains stop and commuters without a car are stuck. Counted for commuters who travel by transit.

register.name: Winter storm
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 66 (34–97) will be snowed in or lose power in a winter storm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Blizzard or lake-effect snow
sub_causes.note: Whiteouts or very deep snow close roads for days. Counted in the winter-storm rate.

sub_causes.name: Roof damage under snow
sub_causes.note: Heavy snow or ice loads a roof until it sags or fails. Counted in the winter-storm rate; clear flat roofs early.

register.name: A household member is arrested or detained
register.frequency_sentence: For households with people the ages of yours, the FBI's counts come to about 7 arrests for every 100 households a year (2023–2025). This counts arrests, not guilt or convictions, and one person arrested twice counts twice.

register.name: Medicine shortage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 39 (18–78) will have a daily medicine they cannot fill for days or weeks because of a shortage in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Hospital supply shock
sub_causes.note: A key hospital supply runs short (IV fluids after Hurricane Helene closed a plant making about 60 % of the US supply in 2024) and planned care is delayed.

register.name: Hurricane
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 37 (21–58) will lose power or have damage from a hurricane or tropical storm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Inland flooding from a tropical storm
sub_causes.note: A weakening hurricane can drop a foot or more of rain far inland (Helene in western North Carolina, 2024), cutting water service for weeks.

register.name: Long illness in the household
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 33 (18–70) will have someone sick at home for weeks in the next ten years.

register.name: Civil unrest
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 26 (10–45) will live under a curfew because of unrest in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Unrest around elections
sub_causes.note: Protests, clashes or curfews around elections or political events.

register.name: Chemical spill or release
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 24 (9–49) will be told not to drink the tap water, or to stay inside, after a chemical spill in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Release from a chemical plant
sub_causes.note: A plant that uses large amounts of toxic or flammable chemicals has a release or explosion (West, Texas, 2013). Counted in the chemical-release rate.

sub_causes.name: Train derailment with chemicals
sub_causes.note: A train carrying chemicals derails and burns or leaks; homes within a mile or two are evacuated (East Palestine, 2023).

sub_causes.name: Tanker truck spill
sub_causes.note: A tanker crash closes roads and may bring an order to stay inside nearby.

sub_causes.name: Pipeline rupture
sub_causes.note: A gas or oil transmission pipeline ruptures and burns or spills; nearby homes are evacuated.

sub_causes.name: Refinery, tank farm or port fire
sub_causes.note: A large industrial fire brings orders to stay inside and smoke for days.

sub_causes.name: Chemical spill into the water supply
sub_causes.note: A spill upstream of a water intake brings a do-not-use order for days (Elk River, West Virginia, 2014). Counted in the chemical-release rate.

register.name: Eviction
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 21 (10–39) will be taken to court and ordered to leave their rented home in the next ten years.

register.name: Cyberattack on services
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 18 (7–39) will lose pharmacy, payment or other services to a computer outage or cyberattack in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Critical software failure
sub_causes.note: A faulty update or cloud outage takes down hospital, airline, bank or 911 systems for a day or more (July 2024). Counted in this rate.

sub_causes.name: Card or bank payment outage
sub_causes.note: Cards, bank apps or cash machines stop for hours to days. Keep some cash in small bills.

register.name: Burst pipe or water leak
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 17 (10–26) will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Sewer backup
sub_causes.note: Sewage backs up through basement drains; standard home policies leave it out unless you add sewer-backup cover.

register.name: Death or disability of an earner
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 16 (10–26) will lose an earner's income to death or disability in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Death in the family
sub_causes.note: A family member who does not earn dies: funeral costs and time off work.

register.name: Pandemic
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 11 (3–23) will live through a pandemic that changes daily life in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Mosquito- or tick-borne outbreak
sub_causes.note: Local dengue or West Nile spread brings spraying and advisories.

sub_causes.name: Local disease outbreak
sub_causes.note: Measles, hepatitis A or Legionnaires' in the community keeps people out of school or work. Check your vaccinations.

sub_causes.name: Bird flu (H5N1)
sub_causes.note: A candidate pandemic strain that so far passes from animals to people, not between people.

register.name: Break-in
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 10 (5–18) will have a break-in in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Identity theft and disaster scams
sub_causes.note: Accounts opened in your name, or fake contractors and FEMA impostors after a disaster. A credit freeze is free.

register.name: Flooding from rivers or heavy rain
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 6 (2–15) will have flood water reach their home in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Flash flood
sub_causes.note: Water rises in minutes on roads and near creeks; most flood deaths are people driving into it. Counted in the flood rate; turn around, don't drown.

sub_causes.name: Basement or street flooding in heavy rain
sub_causes.note: Drains overflow and water or sewage comes up into basements outside the mapped flood zone. It is the outside-the-zone part of the flood rate, higher with a basement.

sub_causes.name: Levee failure or overtopping
sub_causes.note: Counted on the dam and levee card, not here: leveed land is mapped outside the high-risk flood zone.

sub_causes.name: Ice-jam flood
sub_causes.note: River ice jams in late winter and backs water into riverside homes. Counted in the flood rate.

register.name: House fire
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (3–8) will have a house fire, in their home or next door in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
sub_causes.note: Carbon monoxide from a furnace, generator or car builds up indoors, most often after storms when generators run too close to the house. Shown beside fires, not added to them; a CO alarm is the defence.

sub_causes.name: Lithium battery fire
sub_causes.note: E-bike, scooter and power-bank batteries can catch fire while charging; charge them where you can see them.

register.name: Regional blackout
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (1–14) will lose power in a regional blackout that is not caused by weather in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Attack on power substations
sub_causes.note: Gunfire or sabotage at substations can cut power to a county for days (Moore County, North Carolina, 2022). Utilities report about 78 cases of attack, vandalism or theft a year, most with no outage (2019–2023).

sub_causes.name: Cyberattack on the grid
sub_causes.note: Hackers switched off parts of Ukraine's grid in 2015; no US case has cut power. Utilities report about 7 cyber events a year (2019–2023).

register.name: Ice storm
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 (1–11) will lose power or be stuck at home in an ice storm in the next ten years.

register.name: Lightning
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (fewer than 1 to 6) will have lightning damage their home or cut their power in the next ten years.

register.name: Earthquake
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 2 will feel an earthquake strong enough to knock things off shelves in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Liquefaction
sub_causes.note: Wet, sandy ground turns to slurry in strong shaking; pipes and foundations fail. Water outages last longer where it happens.

sub_causes.name: Fire after an earthquake
sub_causes.note: Broken gas lines and low water pressure let fires spread after a big earthquake. Know how to shut off the gas, and leave it to the gas company to turn it back on.

register.name: Drought
register.frequency_sentence: About 9 (2–42) in 1,000 households like yours will face water limits in a drought in the next ten years.

register.name: Attack or threat closes your area
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 490 and 1 in 31 households like yours would have an attack or threat close their area or its transit for half a day or more in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: The Philadelphia-Camden-Wilmington, PA-NJ-DE-MD urban area is one of the 44 urban areas FEMA funds for terrorism preparedness, chosen by the risk the Department of Homeland Security assigns them. It gets about 2.8 in 100 of the money, which is how this estimate weighs your area.

register.name: Tornado
register.frequency_sentence: About 5 (1–15) in 1,000 households like yours will have a tornado damage or cut off their neighborhood in the next ten years.

register.name: Hail
register.frequency_sentence: About 3 (1–8) in 1,000 households like yours will have hail damage their home or car in the next ten years.

register.name: Coastal flooding
register.frequency_sentence: About 3 (1–8) in 1,000 households like yours will have coastal flooding reach their home in the next ten years.

register.name: Nuclear power plant accident
register.frequency_sentence: About 1 in 2,000 (1 in 10,000 to 1 in 500) households like yours will be told to stay inside or leave after a nuclear power plant accident in the next ten years.

register.name: War with attacks on US infrastructure
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 250 and 1 in 13 households like yours would lose power, water or phone service for days to attacks in a war in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: Your county has military sites, a big city, a port or a refinery nearby: the kinds of places attacks on infrastructure aim at.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a break-in (about 10 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Outages of power, water or phones for days, and shortages across the country.

register.name: Financial crisis with bank closures
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 11 households like yours would have banks close for three days or more in a financial crisis in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Your own bank fails
sub_causes.note: Insured deposits (up to $250,000 per person at each bank) move to another bank, usually within days. The FDIC counts about 23 failures a year (2001–2025), most of them small banks.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a pandemic that changes daily life (about 11 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Cards and bank transfers stop for days.
register.what_it_changes: Keep some cash in small bills (already in your plan) and a second account at another bank (free).

register.name: Very large volcanic eruption
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 130 and 1 in 26 households like yours would live through a year or two of higher food prices after a very large eruption somewhere in the world in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A Yellowstone super-eruption
sub_causes.note: Devastation nearby and ash across much of the country. The USGS puts it at about 1 in 730,000 a year.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a regional blackout (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: A year or two of higher food prices and some shortages.

register.name: Severe pandemic
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 21 households like yours would live through a pandemic far deadlier than COVID-19 in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A natural pandemic as deadly as 1918
sub_causes.note: The 1918 flu killed about 675,000 Americans. Records of pandemics over four centuries give the chance.

sub_causes.name: An engineered germ
sub_causes.note: A germ made or changed on purpose. There is no record to count; it is part of the expert range.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a house fire (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Months of disruption, strained hospitals and lost income.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing new: the pandemic row already sizes your food and medicine.

register.name: Severe solar storm
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 2,600 and 1 in 51 households like yours would lose power for days to a severe solar storm in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: Your county is at a middle geomagnetic latitude (about 49°). Solar storms drive the strongest currents into long power lines nearer the magnetic pole, so the chance of a long outage here is about 1.3 times the national average. The ground's conductivity also matters and is not counted.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than an ice storm (about 3 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Power out for days, and longer where large transformers fail.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing beyond your power plan: a solar storm harms long power lines, not phones or radios.

register.name: Nuclear attack
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 3,300 and 1 in 28 households like yours would be in a blast zone or under dangerous fallout in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Limited strike on US territory
sub_causes.note: One or a few weapons on US soil, for example a strike on Guam, Hawaii, Alaska or a West Coast base. It adds to your chance only where your county is a plausible target.

sub_causes.name: A crude nuclear device in a city
sub_causes.note: Heavy damage within about a mile, and everyone within 50 miles told to get inside. It adds to your chance by your metro area's share of FEMA's terrorism-preparedness money.

sub_causes.name: Electromagnetic pulse (EMP) from a high-altitude burst
sub_causes.note: Only as part of a nuclear attack: a burst high above the country could cut power and phones over a wide area and damage some cars and electronics. EPRI's 2019 study found months-long nationwide blackouts unlikely; the claim that most Americans would die is not a published model.

sub_causes.name: Disruption across the country
sub_causes.note: Shortages, power cuts and lost income even far from any target. Shown for everyone and never added to your local chance.

sub_causes.name: A nuclear weapon used elsewhere in the world
sub_causes.note: At home: market shocks, shortages and worry, with no fallout of concern. Never added to your local chance.

location_factor.label: You live in the Philadelphia metro area. Because of its size and importance, a place like this is treated as a likely target in a large nuclear war. That does not mean an attack is likely, only that the danger here would be greater than in most places.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a regional blackout (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Life-threatening: blast or heavy fallout near likely targets.
register.what_it_changes: One free step: pick your shelter spot at home and at work (a basement, or the middle of the building away from windows).

register.name: Power out for months (any cause)
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 31,000 and 1 in 42 households like yours would be without power for two months or more in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A severe solar storm
sub_causes.note: Long outages where large transformers fail; most places would be back within days.

sub_causes.name: EMP from a nuclear attack
sub_causes.note: Only as part of a nuclear attack; EPRI's 2019 study found months-long nationwide blackouts unlikely.

sub_causes.name: Attacks on the grid in a war
sub_causes.note: Cyberattacks, sabotage or missiles on power plants and lines.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than an ice storm (about 3 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: No power for months: water, heat, medicine and money all affected. Puerto Rico waited 328 days after Hurricane Maria.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing to stockpile for months. The long-horizon section lists what helps instead: a water filter with a water source, a way to cook, sanitation.

register.name: Chemical, biological or radiological attack
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 35,000 and 1 in 180 households like yours would be told to stay inside, or to collect medicine at a public site, after a chemical, biological or radiological attack in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Chemical
sub_causes.note: About 3 in 4 such incidents worldwide involve chemicals: shelter inside for hours, or leave the immediate area if told to.

sub_causes.name: Biological
sub_causes.note: A germ spread on purpose (the anthrax letters of 2001): stay home, and collect preventive medicine at a public site if told to.

sub_causes.name: Radiological ("dirty bomb")
sub_causes.note: Shelter inside for hours; the area may stay closed for weeks. None has caused mass casualties anywhere.

location_factor.label: The Philadelphia-Camden-Wilmington, PA-NJ-DE-MD urban area is one of the 44 urban areas FEMA funds for terrorism preparedness, chosen by the risk the Department of Homeland Security assigns them. It gets about 2.8 in 100 of the money, which is how this estimate weighs your area.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than an attack or threat closing your area (about 8 in 1,000 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: An order to stay inside for hours, closed buildings, or medicine handed out at public sites.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing beyond your basics: your three-day supplies cover sheltering inside.

register.name: Mass shooting or bombing
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 250,000 and 1 in 25,000 households like yours would have someone hurt in a mass shooting or bombing in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: The data are too sparse to say where this is more likely, so the chance is the same everywhere.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a nuclear plant accident (about 1 in 2,000 for you in the next ten years).
register.what_it_changes: Nothing to buy. Two free steps: know "run, hide, fight", and learn to stop bleeding.

This number mostly depends on how long boil-water notices from local water problems last (expert estimate) and how often local water and gas problems happen where you live (expert estimate).

buckets.name: Dangerous heat or cold indoors

This number mostly depends on how often cyberattacks on services happen where you live (expert estimate) and how long gaps in medicine from pharmacy or insurer computer outages last (expert estimate).

buckets.name: No phone, internet or card payments

Being ready for 2 days leaves about 9 (5–25) of 100 households like yours facing a longer outage in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how often windstorms happen where you live (expert estimate) and how long phone and payment outages from short storm outages last (expert estimate).

buckets.name: Must leave home quickly

Plan to be away for about 2 days.

buckets.name: Stranded away from home
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 80 (45–100) will have someone stranded away from home at least once in the next 10 years.

The 4-mile (6 km) trip is about an hour on foot; carry about half a litre of water for it in hot weather.
The get-home bag is sized by the walk home at about 3 miles an hour, with about half a litre of water per hour in hot weather.

buckets.name: Medical emergency when help is slow
frequency_sentences: Households like yours average about 2 emergency-room visits a year (national figures).

buckets.name: House fire
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (3–8) will have a home fire at least once in the next 10 years.

buckets.name: Home and personal security
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 35 (15–50) will have a break-in or a nearby curfew at least once in the next 10 years.

buckets.name: Unhealthy air indoors

buckets.name: Loss of income

Renters insurance that pays for somewhere to stay is the main protection if your home becomes unlivable.

items.name: Set up emergency alerts and know how to reach 911
items.why: Free. Gets you ready for leaving home quickly. About 15 of 100 households like yours need this in the next 10 years. Main causes here: house fire and hurricane. Also helps with phone and internet outages, medical emergencies and power cuts.

items.name: Make a household plan and a contact card for each person
items.why: Free. Adds half a day of phone power and news, bringing you to 0.5 of the 2-day goal. About 7 of 100 households like yours lose phone and internet for a day or more in the next 10 years. Main causes here: strong wind and hurricane. Also helps with leaving home quickly and getting home.

items.name: Fire safety at home: alarms, an escape plan, safe cooking and heating
items.why: Free. Gets you ready for a fire at home. About 5 of 100 households like yours need this in the next 10 years. Main cause here: house fire. Also helps with leaving home quickly.

items.name: Water and food know-how: boil water, use your water heater, keep food cold
items.why: Free. Adds 3.5 days of safe water during boil notices for 4 people, bringing you to 3.5 of the 7-day goal. requirements.plain: 4 battery lights: a headlamp or lantern for each person aged 4 and over. Use lights, not candles. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 pack of AA or AAA batteries for the lights and the radio: one pack lasts a household about 7 days. Check which sizes your lights use. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

1 pair of appliance thermometers, one in the fridge and one in the freezer: after a power cut, keep refrigerated food only if it stayed at 40 °F or below, and throw out perishable food that was above 40 °F for 2 hours or more. (Ready.gov)

1 battery power station (about 1,070 Wh each) as an optional upgrade for lights, phones and a radio. Your essential load (phones) is about 45 Wh a day, 140 Wh for 3 days; one station gives about 910 Wh after losses, enough for about 20.2 days of that load. A full-size fridge alone would drain one in about 0.9 days. (retail prices, ENERGY STAR; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: a portable generator can run the fridge and lights through a 3-day outage. It must run outdoors, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and vents, never in a garage, and it needs fuel (see the fuel line). Ask your landlord first. (CDC, Ready.gov, Ready Reckoner research; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: keeping a fridge running takes about 995 Wh a day (a chest freezer about 597) × 3 days = 2,990 Wh. A closed fridge keeps food cold about 4 hours and a full freezer about 48; shelf-stable food avoids the need. (ENERGY STAR, Ready.gov)

For a boil-water notice of up to 7 days: make about 3.3 gallons of drinking water safe each day, about 23.2 gallons in all. To make it safe, boil it for 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 feet), or add 8 drops of 6 % unscented bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25 %) and wait 30 minutes; double the bleach for cloudy or very cold water. A gas stove can boil water while the gas flows; never use a camp stove or grill indoors. (Ready.gov, PetMD, CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

1 bottle of plain unscented bleach (5 to 9 % sodium hypochlorite, not the splashless kind), for making water safe and for cleaning, however long your target is. At about 0.5 mL a gallon, each ounce treats about 60 gallons of clear water (30 if it is cloudy or very cold), so one bottle treats thousands of gallons. Bleach weakens in storage: buy a fresh bottle every 6 months, when you replace the water you store yourself. (CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

If you boil on a camp stove outdoors, about 3.2 lb of propane brings 88 L to a boil (about 25 to 30 L a pound). Never use a camp stove indoors, and keep no more than 2 one-pound cylinders inside. (EIA, local fire code, CDC; some amounts are estimates)
4 people × 1 gallon a day × 3 days = 12 gallons, plus 0.9 gallons for the dog: about 12.9 gallons. Replace water you store yourself every 6 months. (Ready.gov, CDC, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)

Free first step: fill clean drink bottles you already have with tap water, about 6 gallons, the most a household can usually gather this way. Not milk jugs: they leak. Label them and replace the water every 6 months. (Ready Reckoner research, CDC, Ready.gov, Church of Jesus Christ; some amounts are estimates)
A two-bucket toilet for when toilets can't flush: 2 sturdy buckets with a seat, one for pee and one for poo. (RDPO, Oregon OEM)

Toilet bags: about 0.45 heavy garbage bags a person a day (0.3 to 0.6), counting both bags of a double-bagged load: 4 people × 3 days = 6 bags. Fill halfway, tie, double-bag, and store away from food, water, children and pets. Don't put them in curbside trash or bury them unless officials say so. (RDPO, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

Cover material for the poo bucket (sawdust, shredded paper, dry leaves or pet bedding): about 1 cup a person a day (0.5 to 1.5) × 4 people × 3 days = 12 cups, about 0.8 gallons. (RDPO; some amounts are estimates)

2 adults at about 2,262 kcal a day each, 1 person 65 or over at about 2,009 kcal a day and 1 child aged 4 to 12 at about 1,667 kcal a day: about 8,199 kcal a day × 10 days = 82,000 kcal. These are moderately active needs; the form does not ask sex, so men's and women's needs are averaged. Count calories, not servings. (Dietary Guidelines)
As everyday groceries: about $338 for 40 person-days (USDA Thrifty Food Plan, $8.44 a person a day). Buy what you already eat, keep it in the pantry and use the oldest first. (USDA)

As bulk staples such as wheat, rice and beans: about $100 ($2.15 to $2.85 a person a day). Cheapest, but it needs cooking and is short on some vitamins, so it suits months rather than days. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU)

As freeze-dried or dehydrated meals: about $984 ($9 to $39 per 2,000 kcal, so $369 to $1,599). They need about 0.6 gallons of extra water a person a day to prepare. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

A retail "30-day" food kit supplies about 1,290 to 1,730 kcal a day. For the average person here (about 2,050 kcal a day) one lasts about 19 to 25 days, not 30. Compare kits by total kcal. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices)

Dry food for the dog for 10 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog = 7 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the dog for 10 days (10 pet-days, at least a week): what it eats now, in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)

If you cook or boil water on a camp stove: about 0.2 lb of fuel a person a day × 4 people × 10 days = 8 lb, or 16 canisters of 0.5 lb each. Use it outdoors only, never indoors (carbon monoxide). (CDC, Ready Reckoner research, EIA, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)
Toilet paper: about 1 roll a person every 5 days × 4 people × 10 days = 8 rolls. Better still, measure a week's use and double it for two weeks. (Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Soap for 4 person-months: 4 people × 1 month. Each is 250 g of bathing soap and 200 g of laundry soap, about 1,800 g in all. (Sphere)

Period products for 2 cycles each, about 20 products a cycle (15 to 30). The form doesn't ask sex, so the plan counts half of the 2 people aged 13 to 64 who are not pregnant or nursing: 2 cycles' worth, about 40 products. Keep soap, clean underwear and pain relievers with them, and put used products in a separate bag. (CDC, Sphere, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

2 battery fans: 1 for the home plus 1 for the 1 person most at risk from heat (65 and over, babies, pregnancy). Fans help only while it is below 90 °F indoors; above that, go to a cooling centre. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
4 cooling towels, one for each person: wet them and wear them on the neck in a heat wave. (an estimate)
A heat plan: find your nearest cooling centre (dial 2-1-1), pick the coolest room, cover sunny windows, and agree who checks on whom. Never leave people or pets in a closed car. (CDC, Ready.gov)
1 room thermometer in the room where the most vulnerable person sleeps: fans help only while it is below 90 °F indoors, so when it reads higher, go somewhere cooler. (CDC)
4 warm blankets, one for each person: most homes already have them. (Ready.gov, Sphere)
4 sets of warm layers (coat, hat, gloves, dry socks), one for each person. (Ready.gov, CDC)

1 sleeping bag or extra heavy blanket for the person 65 or over, who is most at risk in the cold. For a cold target of 3 days, blankets and warm layers do for everyone else. (Ready.gov, Sphere, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

A cold plan: pick one room to keep warm, close off the others, put towels under doors and cover windows at night. Never heat with a gas oven, grill, camp stove or generator indoors (carbon monoxide). Gas, oil and propane furnaces usually need electricity for their fans and controls, so plan for cold without power. People 65 and over should check the indoor temperature often. A body temperature below 95 °F needs medical help at once. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)

1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 14 days of it on hand. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)

No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)
1 battery or hand-crank radio that gets NOAA Weather Radio, with a tone alert, for warnings when phones and power are down. (Ready.gov, NOAA)
Power banks: 3 phones × about 15 Wh a day (10 to 20) × 3 days without power = 140 Wh. Text instead of calling to save battery. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

3 two-way radios for the 3 people aged 13 and over, to reach each other when phones are down. FRS radios need no licence; GMRS radios reach farther but need a $35 FCC licence that covers the family for 10 years. (FCC; some amounts are estimates)
4 written contact cards, one for each person aged 4 and over: an out-of-area contact, meeting places and key numbers. Phones die; paper does not. (Ready.gov)
1 paper map of your area, marked with meeting places and ways out. Save offline maps on your phone too. (Ready.gov)

Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $100 to start, or enough for about 3 days of basics (food, fuel, medicine) at your own daily spending. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)

4 go-bags, one for each person: a sturdy bag you already own will do. Pack copies of documents, a phone charger, cash, a flashlight, a whistle, a change of clothes and sturdy shoes, and add water, food and medicines from your home supplies rather than buying them twice. You may get only minutes of warning (a local tsunami or a fast fire), so keep the bags packed by the door, and one at work if you work in a danger zone. Practise grabbing them and leaving. Plan where you would stay for about 2 days. (Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Water for the go-bags comes out of the water you store at home, not on top of it: the Red Cross three-day supply for leaving home, about 4 gallons a day for the 4 people × 2 days = 8 gallons. Keep it with the bags or take it as you leave. If you leave on foot, carry what you can (about 2.5 L each) and a filter; the rest goes in the car. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Food for the go-bags comes out of your home food supply, not on top of it: about 8,199 kcal a day × 2 days = 16,400 kcal of food that needs no cooking or refrigeration. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Dietary Guidelines)

1 pet carrier, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine it takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)
Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the dog = 2.2 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the dog = 10 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)
Keep the vehicle at least half full at all times, and fill up when leaving looks likely. (Ready.gov)
1 person may need help to leave quickly: arrange a ride and a helper now, and show them where the medicines and equipment are. (Ready.gov)

Person 1 travels 11.8 miles (19 km) by car to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 3.9 hours. Keep a get-home bag in the car: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Water for person 1's walk home: 3.9 hours × about 0.5 L an hour = 2 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. (FHWA; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 1's walk home: about 400 kcal for 3.9 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)

Person 2 travels 3.7 miles (6 km) by bus or train to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 1.2 hours. Keep a get-home bag at work or in your daily bag: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Water for person 2's walk home: 1.2 hours × about 0.5 L an hour = 0.6 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. (FHWA; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 2's walk home: about 100 kcal for 1.2 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)
1 car emergency kit: jumper cables, a flashlight, warm clothes, a blanket, bottled water and snacks; sand or cat litter in snow country. (Ready.gov)

1 family first-aid kit for 4 people: the Red Cross list for a family of 4 (bandages, gauze, tape, antiseptic wipes, gloves, a breathing barrier, a cold pack, tweezers, an emergency blanket and a thermometer). Add your own medicines and emergency numbers, and replace what you use. (Red Cross)

1 package of each of 4 kinds of non-prescription medicine (a pain reliever, an anti-diarrhea medicine, an antacid and a laxative): one package of each lasts about 14 days for 4 people. That is 4 packages for 10 days. Follow the label, and ask a pharmacist about children's versions. (Ready.gov, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)

N95 masks for wildfire smoke or an outbreak: 1 a day for each of the 4 people aged 4 and over, for 5 days = 20 masks. A well-fitting N95 protects more than a cloth or surgical mask. (CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list). (Red Cross)

Oral rehydration salts for vomiting, diarrhea or heat illness: 3 packets a person for every 2 weeks, at least 2 weeks' worth. For 4 people and 14 days that is 12 packets. Mix each packet into 1 litre of safe water. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
1 bleeding-control kit: a tourniquet and a pressure bandage for serious bleeding, and a Stop the Bleed class so you know how to use them. Serious bleeding can kill before help arrives. (DHS)

A fire escape plan: two ways out of every room, a meeting spot outside, and a practice run with everyone. If anyone sleeps upstairs, check that each bedroom has a second way out, such as a window onto a porch roof or an escape ladder. Test your smoke alarms every month. (Ready.gov)

No carbon monoxide alarm yet: put one on every level where people sleep (2 for a home like yours), with battery backup. Replace them every 5 years or as the maker says. (CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

No fire extinguisher yet: 2 multipurpose (A-B-C) extinguishers, one on each of the 2 floors a home like yours has, the ground-floor one near the kitchen. If your kitchen is on another floor, keep one there too. Learn how to use one before you need it. Small home fires are common: CPSC estimated about 6.6 a year for every 100 households, most of them cooking fires, and fire departments attend only about 3 in 100 of them. (USFA, CPSC; some amounts are estimates)
Swap phone numbers with 2 neighbours and agree who checks on whom after a storm or an outage, when phones and roads may be down. (an estimate)

Savings goal: about 4 months of expenses ($16,800 at $4,200 a month), built up over time and kept apart from the supplies budget. You have about 0.5 months saved now. Planners often suggest 3 to 6 months; the CFPB says it depends on your situation. (FINRA, St. Louis Fed, CFPB)

Copy the 4 parts of FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit: IDs, financial and legal papers (including insurance), medical information, and household contacts. Keep copies in a waterproof, fire-resistant place or with someone you trust, with photos of your home and belongings, and update them once a year. (FEMA)
You have no renters insurance yet: get a quote and decide. Check what it pays if you have to live somewhere else for a while. (FEMA, Ready.gov)

Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings, and renters can buy cover for belongings only. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)
A standard home policy does not cover earthquake damage. Decide whether earthquake insurance is worth its deductible where you live. (Ready.gov)

# Your preparedness packet

**For:** 2 adults, 1 older adult and 1 child, with 1 dog  
**Where:** Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania (ZIP code 19147)  
**Home:** a rented rowhouse, with a basement, city water, gas heat and window air conditioning  
**Plan date:** October 1, 2026  
**Ready for:** very serious disruptions, the kind that come about once in 100 years (the 1-in-100 setting), in today's climate. Water is planned at the basic level, about 1 gallon a person a day.[1]

> Ready Reckoner is an independent, open-source planning aid. It is not official emergency guidance, and not medical, legal or financial advice. Follow instructions from your local officials first.

## Summary

**Where you are now:** getting started. **What is enough for your risks:** two weeks of supplies. At your budget, the plan gets there by month 26 (December 2028).

### The three things that matter most

1. Of 100 households like yours, about 35 (30–55) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years. Be ready to manage about 3 days at home with no power or tap water.
2. Of 100 households like yours, about 55 (30–90) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years. Keep about 10 days of food you normally eat, and 2 weeks of daily medicine on hand.
3. Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (6–30) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. Losing a paycheck is the longest disruption most households face. Aim for about 4 months of expenses in savings over time, apart from this supplies budget.

### Start here

These cost nothing and come first. This month's 8 free steps are all under Your plan.

- [ ] Set up emergency alerts and know how to reach 911
- [ ] Make a household plan and a contact card for each person
- [ ] Fire safety at home: alarms, an escape plan, safe cooking and heating

### What the plan assumes you already have

- [x] A charged mobile phone: alerts, calls and a backup light (3 phones)
- [x] Go-bag for each person: a backpack you pack from your supplies (4 bags)
- [x] Manual can opener (1 opener)
- [x] A cooking pot with a lid (1 pot)
- [x] Three days of the food you normally eat (4 × 3 days of food for one person)
- [x] A warm blanket for each person (4 blankets)
- [x] Warm layers for each person: a coat, hat and gloves (4 sets)
- [x] Towels to wet and cool down (4 towels)

If any is missing, untick "Assume everyday basics" on the Have screen and the plan will add it.

## Your risks

What could reach a household like yours in Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania over the next 10 years: the likeliest events, and the rarer ones that can kill, most likely first. A lost job or a week-long outage is far more likely than a disaster from the movies, and the plan is ordered the same way.

### What to know and do

#### 1. Heat wave

Nearly every household like yours will go through a heat wave in the next ten years (about 4.5 times a year).[2]

**What helps.** Know where you can go to cool off. Dial 2-1-1 to find air conditioning near you.[3] Cover windows with drapes or shades, and weather-strip doors and windows.[4] Take cool showers, wear loose, light-colored clothing, and drink plenty of fluids. Check on family members, older adults and neighbours.[4] Heat can cause power outages, so plan for refrigerated medicines and powered medical devices.[3]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on a fan when it is over 90°F indoors. It can make you hotter.[3] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[4] Heat stroke is an emergency. Signs include a body temperature of 103°F or more, hot, red skin that may be dry or damp, a fast, strong pulse, confusion or passing out. Call 911, move the person somewhere cooler, cool them with cool cloths or a cool bath, and give them nothing to drink.[5]

**How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Based on data.

#### 2. Medical emergency

Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years (about 1.9 times a year).[6]

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[7] If a teen or adult collapses and their heart stops, call 911 and push hard and fast in the center of the chest. This hands-only CPR needs no training. Note where the nearest heart defibrillator (AED) is; it talks you through each step.[8] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[9] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[10] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[11]

**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[12] Do not use expired medicines.[13]

**How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Based on data.

#### 3. Cold wave

Nearly every household like yours will go through a spell of dangerous cold in the next ten years (about once a year).[2]

**What helps.** Keep extra blankets, sleeping bags and warm coats, and pick one room to keep warm.[14] If you cannot keep your home warm, go to a warming center. Dial 2-1-1 to find one.[15] Learn how to keep pipes from freezing, and test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms before winter.[16] Keep a car kit with jumper cables, sand, a flashlight, warm clothes, blankets, water and snacks, and keep the gas tank full.[16] Check on older neighbours often.[14] Know the signs of hypothermia, such as shivering, confusion and slurred speech. A body temperature below 95°F is an emergency. Warm the center of the body first.[16]

**What to avoid.** Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Use generators and grills only outdoors, away from windows.[16] Choose electric space heaters with automatic shut-off, and keep them 3 feet from anything that can burn.[14, 17] Do not overdo it when you shovel snow.[16]

**How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Based on data.

#### 4. Wildfire smoke

Of 100 households like yours, about 98 (88 to nearly all) will go through days of unhealthy wildfire smoke in the next ten years.[18, 19, 20]

**What helps.** If anyone has heart or lung disease, ask their health care provider now what to do on smoky days. If someone has asthma, make sure they have an asthma action plan.[21] Keep at least five days of food and medicine at home, so you can stay in.[22] When smoke is forecast, check the air quality on AirNow or your local news, and set up your clean room.[21] Staying indoors is the best protection. Keep two-strap respirators for anyone who has to go out.[23]

**What to avoid.** Avoid hard exercise while it is smoky.[21] Do not stay in a home that is too hot or still smoky inside: go to a friend's home out of the smoke, or a public cleaner-air shelter.[22]

**How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 5. Burst pipe or water leak

Of 100 households like yours, about 17 (10–26) will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.[20, 24, 25]

**What helps.** Find your main water shut-off valve now, and show everyone how to turn it off. A burst pipe can flood a room quickly.[26, 27] Once a year, check the hoses to the water heater, washing machine, dishwasher and fridge, and replace any that crack or leak. A leak alarm can warn you early.[26] In freezing weather, let a faucet drip at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher.[27] Home and renters policies usually cover burst pipes. Many do not cover a sewer backup unless you add that cover, and floods need their own policy.[26]

**What to avoid.** Never thaw a frozen pipe with an open flame; use a hair dryer. Watch for electric shock around standing water.[27] Do not leave home while the washing machine or dishwasher is running.[26]

**How bad:** Severe. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 6. Death or disability of an earner

Of 100 households like yours, about 16 (10–26) will lose an earner's income to death or disability in the next ten years.[20, 28, 29]

**What helps.** Build an emergency fund a little at a time. The right amount depends on your situation.[30] Planners often suggest three to six months of living expenses, and more if your income varies.[31] Know how to file for unemployment in your state.[32] Keep copies of your financial, legal and medical papers together, with the names of people to call.[33] Write a bare-bones budget you could switch to, and keep a pantry that can stretch a tight month.

**What to avoid.** File soon after losing work: contact your state's unemployment program as soon as you can.[32] Do not keep your emergency fund in investments you would have to sell. A savings account lets you take money out at any time without a penalty.[31]

**How bad:** Very severe. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 7. Flooding from rivers or heavy rain

Of 100 households like yours, about 6 (2–15) will have flood water reach their home in the next ten years.[20, 34]

**What helps.** Look up your address on FEMA's flood maps, and sign up for your community's warnings.[35] Homeowner's insurance does not cover flooding, and a flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start.[35] Renters can buy flood coverage for their belongings.[36] Know how you would get to higher ground or a higher floor.[35]

**What to avoid.** Six inches of moving water can knock you down, and one foot can sweep your car away.[35] Never drive around barriers on a flooded road. The road may have collapsed under the water.[37] Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.[35] Leave if you are told to.[38]

**How bad:** Very severe. **How sure:** Rough data.

#### 8. House fire

Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (3–8) will have a house fire, in their home or next door in the next ten years.[20, 39]

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside every bedroom and on every level, and test them each month.[40] Practice your escape plan twice a year, including finding your way out in the dark.[41] Sleep with bedroom doors closed. Teach children not to hide from firefighters.[41] If there is smoke, crawl low under it to your exit.[41] If you cannot get out, close the door, cover vents and cracks with cloth or tape, call 911, and signal from the window with a light-colored cloth or a flashlight.[41] Insurance and copies of your documents help you recover afterward.[33]

**What to avoid.** Before you open a door, feel the door and the knob. If either is hot, or smoke is coming around it, keep it closed and use your second way out.[41] If a person or pet is still inside, get out and tell firefighters right away.[41] If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll.[41]

**How bad:** Severe. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 9. Earthquake

Of 100 households like yours, about 2 will feel an earthquake strong enough to knock things off shelves in the next ten years.[42]

**What helps.** Practice Drop, Cover and Hold On: drop to your hands and knees, cover your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops.[43] Secure bookcases, water heaters, TVs and other heavy things, and keep heavy objects on low shelves. A standard homeowner's policy does not cover earthquake damage.[43] Store water in case the taps stop.

**What to avoid.** Do not run outside during shaking, and stay away from doorways.[43]

**How bad:** Severe. **How sure:** Mostly data.

### Other risks we checked

| What could happen | Households like yours, the next 10 years | How bad | How sure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Phone or internet outage | about 95 of 100[20, 44] | Minor | Rough data |
| Supply chain disruption | about 85 of 100[20] | Minor | Expert estimate |
| Strong wind | about 85 of 100[2, 20] | Minor | Rough data |
| Job loss | about 80 of 100[45, 46] | Serious | Mostly data |
| Local water or gas outage | about 80 of 100[20, 47] | Minor | Mostly data |
| Stranded in a vehicle | about 80 of 100[20, 48] | Minor | Mostly data |
| Winter storm | about 65 of 100[2, 20] | Minor | Rough data |
| A household member is arrested or detained | about 50 of 100[49] | Serious | Mostly data |
| Medicine shortage | about 40 of 100[20, 50, 51] | Moderate | Mostly data |
| Hurricane | about 35 of 100[20, 52, 53] | Moderate | Mostly data |
| Long illness in the household | about 35 of 100[20] | Serious | Expert estimate |
| Civil unrest | about 25 of 100[20] | Minor | Expert estimate |
| Chemical spill or release | about 25 of 100[20, 54] | Moderate | Mostly data |
| Eviction | about 20 of 100[20, 55] | Serious | Mostly data |
| Cyberattack on services | about 20 of 100[20] | Minor | Expert estimate |
| Pandemic | about 10 of 100[20, 56, 57] | Serious | Rough data |
| Break-in | about 10 of 100[20] | Serious | Expert estimate |
| Regional blackout | about 5 of 100[20] | Moderate | Expert estimate |
| Ice storm | about 3 of 100[2, 20] | Minor | Rough data |
| Lightning | about 2 of 100[20, 52] | Moderate | Rough data |

Fewer than 1 in 100 households like yours, the next 10 years: drought, attack or threat closes your area, tornado, hail, coastal flooding and nuclear power plant accident.[20, 52, 58, 59, 60, 61]

### Rare but severe

Shown apart, so that a tiny chance of a huge loss cannot crowd out everything else or take over the budget.

| What | How likely | How bad |
| --- | --- | --- |
| War with attacks on US infrastructure | Between 1 in 250 and 1 in 13 households like yours would lose power, water or phone service for days to attacks in a war in the next ten years.[20, 62, 63] | Serious |
| Financial crisis with bank closures | Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 11 households like yours would have banks close for three days or more in a financial crisis in the next ten years.[20, 64] | Moderate |
| Very large volcanic eruption | Between 1 in 130 and 1 in 26 households like yours would live through a year or two of higher food prices after a very large eruption somewhere in the world in the next ten years.[20, 65] | Moderate |
| Severe pandemic | Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 21 households like yours would live through a pandemic far deadlier than COVID-19 in the next ten years.[20, 56, 57] | Very severe |
| Severe solar storm | Between 1 in 2,600 and 1 in 51 households like yours would lose power for days to a severe solar storm in the next ten years.[20, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71] | Serious |
| Nuclear attack | Between 1 in 3,300 and 1 in 28 households like yours would be in a blast zone or under dangerous fallout in the next ten years.[20, 59, 62, 63, 72, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78] | Very severe |
| Power out for months (any cause) | Between 1 in 31,000 and 1 in 42 households like yours would be without power for two months or more in the next ten years.[20, 62, 63, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71, 72, 79, 80] | Very severe |
| Chemical, biological or radiological attack | Between 1 in 35,000 and 1 in 180 households like yours would be told to stay inside, or to collect medicine at a public site, after a chemical, biological or radiological attack in the next ten years.[20, 59, 81] | Serious |
| Mass shooting or bombing | Between 1 in 250,000 and 1 in 25,000 households like yours would have someone hurt in a mass shooting or bombing in the next ten years.[20, 82] | Very severe |

**What helps.** Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned.[78] Go to a basement or the middle of a large brick or concrete building. Stay there for 24 hours unless there is a fire or another immediate danger, or officials say it is safe to leave. Radiation levels drop fast during the first 24 hours.[78]

### Notes on these numbers

- These chances are for Philadelphia County as a whole. A home near a river, the coast or a steep slope can face more; the county's average is what the plan uses.
- A nuclear power plant is within 50 miles (80 km), the zone where food and water may be checked; potassium iodide is only for the 10-mile zone.
- Also checked, and under 1 in 100,000 a year here: landslides (fewer than 1 in 1,000,000 a year), wildfires (about 1 in 350,000 a year), dust storms (none recorded here), sinkholes (fewer than 1 in 1,000,000 a year), dam or levee failures (none recorded here), an asteroid or comet impact (fewer than 1 in 1,000,000 a year) and a Yellowstone super-eruption (about 1 in 730,000 a year).
- Heat and cold waves are marked Serious for this household because someone in it is 65 or older; they are most dangerous for households like yours.
- Wildfire smoke is marked Serious for this household because someone in it is 65 or older; smoke harms them most.

## Your targets

How long to be ready for each kind of disruption at the 1-in-100 setting. For any one need, something worse than its target comes in about 1 of every 10 ten-year stretches. Across all your needs together, the chance that at least one runs out is higher, roughly 1 in 3. That is why the plan also gives you ways to cope when a target runs out.[20, 83]

| If this happens | Be ready for | Outside help likely arrives | Mostly back to normal | Enough at |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No grid power at home | about 3 days (up to 7 days) | about 3 days | about 6 days | three days |
| Tap water must be treated | about 7 days (5 days to 2 weeks) | not known | not known | two weeks |
| No tap water at all | about 3 days (2–7) | not known | not known | three days |
| Can't get to a store | about 10 days (7 days to 1 month) | not known | not known | two weeks |
| Dangerous heat or cold indoors | about 3 days (2–5) | about 3 days | about 6 days | three days |
| Medication and medical-supply continuity | about 2 weeks (10 days to 1 month) | not known | not known | two weeks |
| No phone, internet or card payments | about 2 days (up to 5 days) | not known | not known | three days |

The range in brackets shows how uncertain each target is. "Not known": there are no restoration records for the event behind that target.

### No grid power at home: about 3 days (up to 7 days)

**What helps.** Have a flashlight for each person.[84] Keep a battery or hand-crank radio, and a backup battery for each phone.[85] Keep the fridge and freezer closed. A closed fridge keeps food cold for about four hours, and a full freezer for about two days.[84] If someone relies on a powered medical device or cold medicine, make a plan with their medical provider now.[84] Join your power company's medical program for early warnings of outages, but plan as if your power will not come back first.[86] Many cities and counties keep a voluntary registry of people who may need help; ask yours.[10] A battery power station burns no fuel, so it makes no carbon monoxide.[87]

**What to avoid.** Never run a generator inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. Keep it outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[87] Put a carbon monoxide alarm on every level of your home.[84] Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion can mean carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone outside to fresh air, then call 911.[88] Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Unplug electronics, because the power can come back with a surge that damages them.[84] Treat every downed power line as live: stay at least 30 feet from it and anything it touches, and call 911.[89] If one falls on your car, stay inside unless the car is on fire.[90]

### Tap water must be treated: about 7 days (5 days to 2 weeks)

**What helps.** Use bottled water, or bring clear water to a rolling boil for one minute. Boil for three minutes above 5,000 feet, then let it cool.[91] If you cannot boil water, add plain unscented bleach: 8 drops of 6% bleach or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach per gallon. Stir, and wait 30 minutes.[91] Use boiled or bottled water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, baby formula and ice. If the power is out too, a camp stove works, but only outdoors.[87]

**What to avoid.** Do not use water or ice from the fridge dispenser while a notice is on. Boil tap water even if it went through a home filter or a filter pitcher.[92] Boiling does not help if the notice warns of chemicals. That is a do-not-drink notice, and you need stored or bottled water instead.[92, 93]

### No tap water at all: about 3 days (2–7)

**What helps.** Store at least one gallon per person per day, for drinking and keeping clean.[1] Fill clean bottles or jugs with tap water and replace it every six months.[94] You can pick a level in the plan. About 3 liters a day covers drinking to survive, one gallon is the basic default, and about 4 gallons (15 liters) is the humanitarian minimum for drinking, cooking and washing.[95] A tank water heater holds 20 to 80 gallons of clean water.[96, 97] For long outages, a filter and a source of raw water go further than more jugs.[83] Filters do not remove viruses, so add a disinfectant such as chlorine dioxide after filtering.[93] A two-bucket toilet keeps waste safe when toilets cannot flush.[98]

**What to avoid.** Do not store water in containers that held chemicals.[94] Milk jugs seal poorly and turn brittle.[99] Never drink pool or spa water. Use it only for washing and cleaning.[97] After a flood, do not drink from a private well until it has been disinfected and tested. Your health department can tell you how.[100]

### Can't get to a store: about 10 days (7 days to 1 month)

**What helps.** Keep extra food that needs no refrigeration, cooking or water, and choose foods your family will eat.[101] Use the oldest cans first and replace them as you go.[102] Buy a little at a time. Ready.gov asks people to buy supplies slowly, so everyone can get what they need.[103] Keep a manual can opener.[101] The plan counts food in calories, not servings. Many "30-day" meal kits hold only about 1,300 to 1,700 calories a day.[104] That is less than most adults need.[105] Store food somewhere cool and dry. Below 85°F is best.[102]

**What to avoid.** Do not buy everything at once. It strains your budget and the store. Do not buy or eat from cans that bulge, leak, are rusted or are deeply dented.[102] Do not trust a kit's "days" label. Check the calories on the package instead.

### Dangerous heat or cold indoors: about 3 days (2–5)

**What helps.** See "Heat wave" and "Cold wave" under Your risks.

### Medication and medical-supply continuity: about 2 weeks (10 days to 1 month)

**What helps.** Refill early, while you still have a week left. The Red Cross suggests keeping a 7-day supply, and Florida advises at least two weeks.[106, 107] Ask your doctor, pharmacist and drug plan how to build an emergency supply, such as a 90-day fill.[10, 108] Keep a written list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies.[10] Many states let pharmacists give an emergency refill, but the rules differ.[109] After a declared disaster, a federal program can help people without insurance replace prescriptions.[110] People with diabetes should pack supplies for at least 1 to 2 weeks: syringes or pen needles, a glucose meter with test strips and spare batteries, and glucose tablets.[111, 112] Insulin in its original vial or pen, opened or not, keeps working for up to 28 days at 59°F to 86°F. In an outage, keep it below 86°F in the shade or a cooler, never frozen.[113, 114] For other medicines that need a fridge, ask your pharmacist now how long each keeps out of it, and write the answer on your medicine list.[84]

**What to avoid.** Do not throw insulin away after a day without power. If it gets hotter than 86°F and you have nothing else, use it, and replace it as soon as you can.[113] Never use insulin that has frozen or looks unusual, with particles, clumps, crystals or a changed color.[113, 115] Do not use expired medicines. Weak antibiotics can fail to treat an infection.[13] Do not share antibiotics or save them for later.[12]

### No phone, internet or card payments: about 2 days (up to 5 days)

**What helps.** Turn on emergency alerts on every phone. They are free, and you do not need to sign up.[116] Keep a battery or hand-crank radio and a NOAA Weather Radio with a tone alert.[85] NOAA Weather Radio has more than 1,000 transmitters covering all 50 states.[117] Write important phone numbers on paper, not only in your phone.[118] Pick an out-of-state contact everyone can text, and a place to meet if you are separated.[43] Keep some cash in small bills, because ATMs and credit cards may not work.[119] License-free two-way radios (FRS) let family members talk over short distances without a phone network.[120]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on one source of news. Do not assume you can text 911 everywhere. It is not available in every area, so call 911 if you can.[11]

### Must leave home quickly

**What helps.** See the steps under Family plan.

**What to avoid.** Many people wait to check with others before they act on a warning.[121] Always follow the instructions of local officials, and leave early enough to avoid being trapped by bad weather.[122] Never walk or drive through floodwater. Six inches of moving water can knock you down.[35]

### Stranded away from home

**What helps.** See the steps under Family plan.

**What to avoid.** Do not force down water when you are not thirsty. Too much water can be harmful.[123] In heat, do not drink more than 6 cups an hour.[124] If you are stuck in a car in a snowstorm, staying in the car is often safest. Run the engine about 10 minutes an hour with a window cracked, and keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow.[14]

### Medical emergency when help is slow

**What helps.** See "Medical emergency" under Your risks.

### House fire

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside sleeping areas and on every level of your home. Test them every month.[40] Some fire departments and the Red Cross install them for free.[40, 125] If you rent, ask your landlord to put them in.[126] Make an escape plan with two ways out of each room, and practice it twice a year.[41] Cooking left alone is the top cause of kitchen fires that spread beyond the pan, so stay with your cooking. Keep a pan lid or baking sheet nearby to cover a pan that catches fire.[127] Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet from heaters, fireplaces and candles.[17] A multipurpose extinguisher labeled "A-B-C" works on most home fires.[128]

**What to avoid.** If a person or pet is still inside, get out, call 911, and tell firefighters where they are.[41] Never heat your home with an oven.[17] Turn off space heaters when you leave the room or go to bed.[17] Replace 9-volt alarm batteries at least once a year.[40] If you smell gas or hear hissing, get everyone out without touching switches or phones, then call 911 and the gas company from a safe distance.[129, 130] Only a professional should turn the gas back on.[130]

### Home and personal security

**What helps.** Burglars look for homes that are easy targets. Lock up, and light the places where someone could hide.[131] Work with your neighbours to look out for each other.[131] Protect key accounts with a password manager and two-step login.[132] Learn a simple way to handle a tense moment: notice what is happening, say hello, judge the risk, and get help if you need it.[133] If an attack happens in a public place, getting away is the top priority.[134]

**What to avoid.** After a disaster, be careful with people who show up offering fast repairs or help for a fee. Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.[135] Do not hide a spare key under the doormat or a planter. Leave it with a trusted neighbour.[131]

### Contacts and meeting places

- **Make a household plan and a contact card for each person.** Agree how you will reach each other, where you will meet if you are separated, and who picks up the children (Ready.gov). Pick one out-of-state contact everyone texts to say they are safe, since texts often get through when calls do not, and write key numbers on a card for each wallet or bag (Ready.gov). ### Leaving home: triggers and routes

About 15 of 100 households like yours have to leave home quickly at least once in 10 years. Warning can be 1 minute to 3 days ahead. Plan to be away for about 2 days.[20, 34, 39, 47, 52, 53, 54]

- **Plan how you would leave: zone, routes, destination and triggers.** Look up your evacuation zone and routes on your state and county emergency management websites, mark two routes on a paper map, and pick where you would go, pet-friendly if you have pets (Ready.gov). For each likely hazard, write a go-or-stay card and an if-then trigger, such as 'If our zone gets an evacuation warning, we leave within 30 minutes.' Plans written in if-then form make people more likely to follow through.[85, 121, 122, 148, 149, 150, 151, 152]
- **Keep your vehicle ready: half a tank, a charged battery, a good spare.** Keep at least half a tank of gas at all times and a full tank when an evacuation looks likely (Ready.gov); if you drive an electric car, keep it charged through storm season and pick destinations within its range (Hillsborough County, Florida). Check the spare tire with the others each month, and keep a phone charging cable in the car (NHTSA). Run the engine only outdoors, never in a garage (CDC).[16, 87, 122, 140, 153, 154, 155, 156]

- **Practice: ten-minute drills and the first things to do.**

#### Drills and if-then plans

**If-then plans.** An if-then plan links a trigger to an action: "If the county issues an evacuation warning for our zone, we leave within 30 minutes." Plans written this way help people follow through.[151] When a warning comes, people often wait to confirm it with others before they act.[121] A trigger you agreed on earlier leaves less to decide in the moment. Write one for each likely hazard, and add who picks up the children and where you will meet.[146]

**Drills.** In New Zealand, people who took part in earthquake drills knew the right actions better, used them more during real shaking, and did more to prepare.[157] Among people who got out of the World Trade Center on 9/11, those with earlier emergency training were less likely to develop PTSD.[158] Practice your fire escape plan twice a year.[41] Other ten-minute drills: Drop, Cover and Hold On, a night without power, grabbing the go-bag against a timer, and sealing a room to shelter in place.[152]

**What to avoid.** Do not skip drills because they feel silly. Each one you finish counts toward your plan.

### Children

#### Talking with children about emergencies

**Before anything happens.** Let children help build the kit and practice the plan.[159] Make sure each child knows your family meeting place and has a contact card.[146] Practice the fire escape plan together twice a year.[41]

**When something happens.** Start by asking what they already know and what questions they have. Give simple, concrete facts without scary details. For a young child, that might be: "A tree branch fell on the power lines, so the lights are off." Tell them about the many people working to help, and the steps being taken to keep them safe.[160]

**What to avoid.** Limit news coverage. If children watch, watch with them and answer their questions.[160] Reassure them when you honestly can, but do not give false reassurance. Let them know it is all right to be upset. If you feel overwhelmed, get support from another adult first. Helping others in the community can ease a child's sense of helplessness.[160]

Keep a spare battery for a power wheelchair or other assistive device if you can, and ask local groups for help buying one if you cannot.[10, 161]

### Pets and animals

- Dry food for the dog for 10 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog = 7 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)[2, 20, 52, 53, 56, 57, 140, 149, 150, 177]
- 1 pet carrier, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine it takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)[122, 150]
- Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the dog = 2.2 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)[140, 150, 178]
- Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the dog = 10 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)[150]

### Stress and mental health

#### Stress, mental health and the 988 line

**What helps.** Save 988 in every phone. It offers free, judgment-free support 24/7 for mental health, substance use and more, by call, text or chat.[179] After a disaster, the Disaster Distress Helpline offers crisis counseling 24/7 to anyone in emotional distress. Call or text 1-800-985-5990.[180] Write a short calm plan: what you might feel, what helps you, and who you will call.[152] Oregon's 2 Weeks Ready program even includes practicing mindfulness as a step in getting prepared.[181]

**What to avoid.** Do not keep the news on all day. No one, adult or child, benefits from graphic details or disturbing images.[160] Reach out before things feel unbearable. The 988 line supports people in emotional distress as well as in crisis.[179]
